subject.title: To the Censorious Ones
subject.author: Anne Waldman
subject.text: I'm coming up out of the tomb, Men of War Just when you thought you had me down, in place, hidden I'm coming up now Can you feel the ground rumble under your feet? It's breaking apart, it's turning over, it's pushing up It's thrusting into your point of view, your private property O Men of War, Censorious Ones! get ready big boys get ready I'm coming up now I'm coming up with all that was hidden Get ready, Big Boys, get ready I'm coming up with all you wanted buried, All the hermetic texts with stories in them of hot & dangerous women Women with lascivious tongues, sharp eyes & claws I've been working out, my muscles are strong I'm pushing up the earth with all you try to censor All the iconoclasm & bravado you scorn All the taunts against your banner & salute I'm coming up from Hell with all you ever suppressed All the dark fantasies, all the dregs are coming back I'm leading them back up now They're going to bark & scoff & rage & bite I'm opening the box boo !

title: The Poem That Addressed a Senator by Name
standfirst: In 1990, while Jesse Helms was getting four performance artists' federal grants vetoed for indecency, Anne Waldman wrote a poem she sometimes performed as "Open Address to Senator Jesse Helms" — and built it out of exactly the women the censors wanted gone.

sections.heading: A Poem With Two Names
sections.body: In print this poem is called "To the Censorious Ones," occasionally with the subtitle "Jesse Helms & Others." On stage, Anne Waldman sometimes announced it as "Open Address to Senator Jesse Helms." The surviving recording comes from the Naropa Audio Archive of live performances given at the Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics, and the scholars who discuss it on the podcast PoemTalk date the reading to around 1990 from internal evidence in the tape itself. A poem that needs a different name for the room than for the page is not a general complaint about prudishness. The "you" running through it is not rhetorical — "can you feel the ground rumble under your feet?" asks someone specific enough to feel an actual floor move, and the poem names its target's camp outright: "O Men of War, Censorious Ones!"

sections.heading: What the Address Was Actually Answering
sections.body: By 1990, Jesse Helms had already changed how the federal government pays for art. After the 1989 uproar over Andres Serrano's and Robert Mapplethorpe's work, Helms and Senator Alfonse D'Amato led a group of senators demanding changes at the National Endowment for the Arts; that March the NEA began attaching an obscenity clause to its grant contracts. In June 1990, chairman John Frohnmayer vetoed grants to four performance artists — Karen Finley, Holly Hughes, Tim Miller and John Fleck — overriding his own theater panel's recommendation that they be funded. The artists sued, won in 1993 and were paid, then lost at the Supreme Court in 1998, when *National Endowment for the Arts v. Finley* upheld Congress's right to weigh "general standards of decency" in federal arts funding. Waldman herself had, at various points, received NEA grants. The veto was only months old when she recorded a poem naming the man behind it.

sections.heading: The Women She Says She Knew
sections.body: The poem's most striking line is an inventory, not a flourish: "hermetic texts with stories in them of hot & dangerous women," women with "lascivious tongues, sharp eyes & claws." Waldman has given an account of exactly who those women were. Describing Greenwich Village in the early 1960s, where she grew up, she has said she knew "interesting and creative women who became junkies for their boyfriends, who stole for their boyfriends, who concealed their poetry and artistic aspirations, who slept around to be popular, who had serious eating disorders, who concealed their unwanted pregnancies raising money for abortions on their own" — women who "lived secret or double lives because love and sexual attraction to another woman was an anathema," women sent to mental hospitals by abusive fathers. "Some ran away from home," she has said. "Some committed suicide." Read against that testimony, the poem's claim to be dragging up "all you wanted buried" is not myth-making for its own sake. It is a specific ledger.

sections.heading: A Life Built on the Room, Not the Page
sections.body: The fight was personal in a concrete way, because Waldman's whole method depended on the room a decency clause could close. She directed the Poetry Project at St. Mark's Church in-the-Bowery from 1968 to 1978, and in 1974 co-founded the Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics at Naropa with Allen Ginsberg, who called her his "spiritual wife," and Chögyam Trungpa. She considers performance a "ritualized event in time" and credits her own "Fast Speaking Woman" as the poem that fixed that belief in her. Asked years later how she decides when a poem needs to be chanted rather than read quietly, she said plainly: "some things are written for protest. They have the need to arise." An amendment policing what a federally funded stage could show was never, for her, an abstract free-speech question. It targeted the only form she had ever fully trusted.

sections.heading: Rising From the Tomb, Then Undercutting It With a Shout
sections.body: The poem's engine is a single claim, repeated and loaded differently each time: "I'm coming up." It comes up out of a tomb, then "from Hell," retrieving in turn "all that was hidden," "all you wanted buried," "all the dark fantasies, all the dregs." It borrows the shape of more than one myth without settling on any — a woman opening a box she was told to leave shut, a figure returning from the underworld with exactly what the underworld was supposed to keep. The PoemTalk panel reads it as a deliberate revival of "myths of the woman rising from below, coming up, coming back, and opening the box," calling the poem's central gesture — "thrusting into [the censor's] point of view" — writerly and political at once, in equal measure. But where a myth would end on revelation, Waldman ends on a taunt. Twenty-odd lines of rising prophecy collapse into one word: "boo." It is a strange note to end an address to a sitting senator on, and that is the point. What Helms was legislating against was never going to announce itself solemnly.
